title: Roman to Integer
description: Brute force to optimized: a hardcoded list of subtractive pairs versus a uniform right to left comparison rule.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s representing a Roman numeral, convert it to its integer value. Roman numerals normally add symbol values together, except when a smaller value symbol appears directly before a larger one, in which case it is subtracted instead.

blocks.text: Given a string s representing a Roman numeral, convert it to its integer value. Roman numerals normally add symbol values together, except when a smaller value symbol appears directly before a larger one, in which case it is subtracted instead.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading an Old Clock Face
blocks.text: Like reading Roman numerals on an old clock face, where most symbols are simply added together left to right, but a few specific pairings, like IV instead of IIII, use a smaller numeral placed just before a larger one to signal subtraction.

blocks.caption: Each symbol adds its value, except a smaller value placed before a larger one subtracts

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Three \"I\" symbols, each worth 1, simply added together","1 + 1 + 1","no symbol here is smaller than one appearing after it, so nothing subtracts"],["Answer","3","a plain sum of three ones"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["L is 50, V is 5, then three I symbols each worth 1","50 + 5 + 1 + 1 + 1","every symbol here is at least as large as the one that follows it, so everything adds"],["Answer","58","a plain sum of all five symbol values"]]}

blocks.text: This uses three subtractive pairs at once, CM (900), XC (90), and IV (4), alongside a plain M (1000), giving 1000 + 900 + 90 + 4, or 1994.
It helps to ask what actually makes a pair like IV subtractive, rather than treating it as one of a fixed list of exceptions to memorize.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force hardcodes exactly six known subtractive pairs and checks the string against that fixed list, which works, but treats subtraction as a set of memorized exceptions rather than identifying the actual rule behind it.

Observation 2: The real rule is simpler and fully general: a smaller value symbol placed directly before a larger one always signals subtraction, no matter which two specific symbols are involved, not just the six commonly listed pairs.

Observation 3: Reading the string from right to left turns that rule into a single running comparison, since scanning backward means the symbol just processed is always available as a running "largest value seen so far" to compare the current symbol against.

Observation 4: Any symbol smaller than that running largest value must be a subtractive symbol relative to whatever comes after it, and any symbol at least as large simply adds and becomes the new largest, confirmed by tracing s equal to "MCMXCIV" right to left through to the correct total, 1994.
Recognizing that "smaller before larger means subtract" is a single general rule, not a fixed list of exceptions, is what replaces a hardcoded lookup table with one uniform right to left comparison.

Keep a fixed list of exactly the six known subtractive two character pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM) and their values. At every position, first check whether the next two characters exactly match one of these six special pairs; if so, add that pair's value and skip ahead two characters. Otherwise, add the single current symbol's value and move ahead one character.

items: At each position, check the next two characters against the fixed list of six subtractive pairs.
If they match one of the six pairs, add that pair's value and advance two positions.
Otherwise, add the current single symbol's value and advance one position.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The six subtractive pairs are checked first at every position, since they must be consumed as a unit of two characters, not one at a time.
Falling through to the single symbol lookup handles every other position, where no special pairing applies.
The position advances by either one or two characters depending on which branch is taken, ensuring every character is consumed exactly once overall.

blocks.text: Every valid Roman numeral is built from either a single symbol or one of exactly six known subtractive pairs, so checking against this fixed list correctly handles every case.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since checking against 6 fixed pairs is constant work per position.
Space: O(1), for the two small fixed lookup tables.

Limitation: hardcoding exactly six special two character pairs is fragile and does not reveal the actual underlying rule (a smaller value symbol appearing before a larger one always means subtract), which generalizes more cleanly than a fixed list of exceptions.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is fragile: it treats subtraction as a property of six specific memorized symbol pairs, rather than a general comparison rule.

What the underlying rule actually is: any symbol smaller than the one immediately following it is subtracted, and this is true regardless of which two specific symbols are involved.

What reading right to left unlocks: scanning backward means the previously processed symbol is always exactly the comparison point needed, no lookahead or special pairing logic required.

The core idea: compare each symbol, scanned right to left, against the largest value seen so far, subtracting when smaller and adding (while updating that largest value) otherwise.

Scan the string from right to left instead, keeping track of the largest symbol value seen so far (which is always the previous symbol, since scanning backward). For each new symbol, if its value is smaller than that running largest value, it must be a subtractive symbol, so subtract it; otherwise add it, and update the running largest value. This single uniform rule replaces the need for any hardcoded list of special pairs.
Scan right to left, comparing each symbol to the largest one seen so far.

blocks.caption: Optimized: scan right to left, subtracting whenever a symbol is smaller than the largest seen so far

blocks.text: This works because scanning right to left guarantees that, at the moment any symbol is examined, the running largest value is exactly the value of the symbol that follows it in the original string, so comparing against it correctly reproduces the "smaller before larger means subtract" rule for every position, without needing to look ahead.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The current symbol is smaller than the running largest value","Its value is subtracted from the total","A subtractive pair, of any two symbols, not just the six memorized ones, is correctly handled"],["The current symbol is at least as large as the running largest value","Its value is added, and it becomes the new largest value going forward","Every plain, non subtractive symbol correctly contributes its full value"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass through the string.
Space: O(1), a single fixed size lookup table of 7 symbol values.

blocks.text: Both approaches run in linear time, but the right to left comparison uniformly captures the actual rule behind Roman numeral subtraction, rather than memorizing six special case pairs, making it less error prone and easier to extend if the symbol set ever changed.

items: Scanning left to right while trying to look ahead for subtractive pairs, which is more error prone than the clean right to left comparison against a running largest value.
Forgetting to update the running largest value after adding a symbol, which breaks the comparison for every symbol that follows.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single symbol string","Trivially returns that symbol's own value."],["A string with no subtractive pairs at all, like \"III\" or \"LVIII\"","Every symbol is simply added."]]}

blocks.text: Explain the right to left insight clearly: reading backward means the previous symbol processed is always the correct comparison point for deciding whether the current symbol should add or subtract.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid hardcoding the six special pairs", think: scan right to left, comparing each symbol to the largest one seen so far.
If the interviewer says "why does scanning backward help", think: the previously processed symbol is always exactly the correct comparison point for the current one.
If the interviewer says "what about the reverse problem, integer to Roman", think: greedily subtract the largest possible symbol or pair value repeatedly, the mirror image of this problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force (hardcoded pairs): O(n) time, O(1) space. Optimized (right to left comparison): O(n) time, O(1) space, with a simpler and more general rule.

items: Pattern: a right to left scan, comparing each symbol to the largest value seen so far, rather than a hardcoded list of subtractive pairs.

Core Idea: a symbol smaller than the one that follows it always signals subtraction, and scanning right to left makes "the symbol that follows it" always immediately available as a running largest value.
Time: O(n) for both approaches.
Space: O(1) for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: Roman numeral subtraction is one general comparison rule, not six special cases to memorize.
Interview Difficulty: both solutions are simple to code; explaining why the right to left version generalizes better is the detail that shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: scan backward, subtract when smaller than the largest seen so far, add and update otherwise.
